PullRequest.Body:

re-adding all of https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/230978/files

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The new hover is registered on the renderer's lifetime store, while the surrounding click/focus listeners are correctly registered on markdownPart. setupManagedHover stores the target in HoverService._managedHovers and installs several DOM listeners until its returned disposable is disposed.
Findings.PerformanceResource: detached request markdown DOM nodes, managed-hover objects, map entries, timers, and DOM event listeners
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Retained objects grow with every request markdown render, including repeated virtualized-row renders while scrolling and checkpoint-driven rerenders, for the lifetime of the chat renderer.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: unbounded retained memory and increasing GC pressure during long chat sessions and repeated history scrolling
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before the change, request markdown rendering did not create this managed hover, so disposing a virtualized markdown part did not leave a hover-service entry retaining its DOM node.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Each render creates a managed hover but registers it with `this._register`, tying cleanup to the whole ChatListItemRenderer instead of the short-lived markdownPart.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added RIGHT-side call `this._register(this.hoverService.setupManagedHover(... markdownPart.domNode ...))` explicitly extends each per-render hover to renderer lifetime.
Findings.Title: Dispose request hovers with their markdown parts
Findings.Impact: Scrolling through or rerendering a long conversation leaves every old request DOM node and its hover listeners retained until the entire chat widget is destroyed, rather than reclaiming them when rows leave the viewport.
Findings.Evidence: renderMarkdown creates a new ChatMarkdownContentPart per rendered request. Its other listeners use markdownPart.addDisposable, but the added hover uses renderer-level _register. HoverService.setupManagedHover inserts targetElement into a strong Map and removes it only in the returned disposable; the existing ChatMarkdownRenderer pattern keeps these hovers in a render-result DisposableStore.
Findings.Recommendation: Register the managed hover with `markdownPart.addDisposable(...)` so virtualization and content-part replacement dispose the hover and release its target immediately.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The added equality check is directly inverted, and the traced response-change listener synchronously calls updateCodeBlockTextModels, which lexes the complete response with marked before widget event coalescing occurs. The only magnitude uncertainty is typical conversation length and response size.
Findings.PerformanceResource: CPU work for markdown lexing and code-block model updates across prior responses
Findings.PerformanceScaling: On both entering and leaving edit mode, work grows with the number and total text size of unchanged responses before the edited request; editing a late request reparses nearly the entire conversation twice.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: increased input latency and UI-thread CPU/GC pressure when starting or ending request editing in long chats
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this change, checkpoint events and the per-response session listeners did not exist, so clicking or canceling request editing did not route historical response content through ChatViewModel.updateCodeBlockTextModels.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Each response subscribes to setCheckpoint and treats equality (`old === new`) as a change. Unchanged responses therefore fire _onDidChange, and ChatViewModel synchronously re-lexes every complete response before accumulated UI updates can coalesce.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added RIGHT-side line `const didChange = this._shouldBeBlocked === isDisabled;` makes unchanged checkpoint state trigger response change events; this entire checkpoint listener is new in the PR.
Findings.Title: Avoid reparsing every unchanged response on checkpoint changes
Findings.Impact: Editing a request near the end of a long conversation synchronously reparses all preceding response markdown on both edit start and edit end, causing visible pauses as history size and response length grow.
Findings.Evidence: ChatResponseModel's added listener computes `didChange` with equality and fires for unchanged responses. ChatViewModel.onAddResponse handles every such event by calling updateCodeBlockTextModels for complete responses; that method runs marked.lexer over the full response and updates each code block. ChatWidget only coalesces downstream view events, so this parsing has already happened per response.
Findings.Recommendation: Update blocked state through the single checkpoint model event without emitting content-change events per response, or at minimum use inequality and a distinct metadata-only change reason that skips updateCodeBlockTextModels.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: createInput is called for every edit and the new input plus child instantiation service are added to ChatWidget's lifetime DisposableStore. DisposableStore retains registered values in a Set until delete/clear, even when callers invoke dispose directly; the PR never deletes these per-edit values.
Findings.PerformanceResource: disposed ChatInputPart/editor object graphs, child instantiation services, context-key scopes, DOM references, and per-input subscription disposables
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Retained state grows by one heavyweight ChatInputPart, one scoped service, and multiple widget-level subscriptions for every request-edit cycle until the ChatWidget itself is destroyed.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: steadily increasing retained memory and GC pressure in a long-lived chat panel after repeated request edits
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Previously createInput constructed the primary ChatInputPart once for the widget, so widget-lifetime registration matched the resource lifetime.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The edit branch now constructs a fresh inline ChatInputPart on every clicked request and registers it and its scoped instantiation service in the widget's lifetime store. Edit completion calls `this.input.dispose()`, but that does not remove the object from the parent DisposableStore's Set; createInput and clickedRequest also add each edit's subscriptions to the same lifetime store.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added RIGHT-side assignment `this.inlineInputPart = this._register(scopedInstantiationService.createInstance(ChatInputPart, ...))` places a per-edit resource in a widget-lifetime owner.
Findings.Title: Own inline inputs in an edit-scoped disposable store
Findings.Impact: Repeatedly editing requests in the same chat retains all prior inline editor/input graphs even after each editor is closed, so memory use grows with edit count rather than returning to a stable baseline.
Findings.Evidence: clickedRequest invokes createInput for every edit. The added line wraps each inlineInputPart in this._register, and the preceding added line does the same for its child service. DisposableStore.add stores disposables in `_toDispose`; only delete/clear removes them. Submit/cancel paths directly dispose the input but never delete either object from the widget store.
Findings.Recommendation: Use a MutableDisposable or dedicated edit-scoped DisposableStore containing the child service, inline input, and all per-edit listeners; clear that store from the common edit teardown path instead of registering each edit on ChatWidget.

Scenarios.Scenario: Render and scroll a long chat history containing editable request rows
Scenarios.CriticalPath: ListView synchronously virtualizes rows during scroll; ChatListItemRenderer creates request markdown and its hover before the row is usable. No subprocess, IPC, filesystem, database, or network operation is on this path.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of request markdown renders, including rerenders and rows encountered while scrolling.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Single UI-thread rendering and disposal; list template caching reuses row templates, but each markdown render creates a distinct managed hover.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The list row/template cache is warm during scrolling, but the new HoverService map entry is not evicted when the markdown part is disposed, so warm virtualization still accumulates retained targets.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: renderer-level ownership and HoverService's strong target map/removal semantics are explicit.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Typical request count and scrolling depth vary, but retention is monotonic per render until the widget is destroyed.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable cleanup-lifecycle regression: per-render hover DOM and listeners outlive virtualized rows.

Scenarios.Scenario: Start or cancel editing a previous request in a long conversation
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The click/focus path synchronously sets a checkpoint, dispatches session events, reparses response markdown/code blocks, diffs the tree, and creates or tears down an inline ChatInputPart before interaction settles. No external process or I/O boundary is required.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number and aggregate text size of responses before the edited request; a late request approaches the entire conversation.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Single UI thread. Widget view events are accumulated, but each response's markdown lexing occurs synchronously before that coalescing.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: There is no parse cache for updateCodeBlockTextModels; unchanged complete responses are lexed again on each checkpoint transition. Existing code-block models do not avoid the lexer pass.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the equality condition fires for unchanged responses, and the response listener directly reaches marked.lexer.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact latency depends on conversation length and markdown size, but the affected response set and full-text parse mechanism are established.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable repeated-work regression: unchanged historical responses are reparsed on both edit entry and exit.

Scenarios.Scenario: Repeatedly edit and close previous requests in one long-lived chat panel
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Each edit synchronously constructs a child instantiation scope and ChatInputPart/editor; close/submit disposes the input, but widget-lifetime ownership retains the registered objects. No external boundary is involved.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of request-edit cycles during the ChatWidget lifetime.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Sequential edit cycles on the UI thread; no limiter is relevant because retained state accumulates across cycles rather than concurrently.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No reusable inline-input cache or replaceable owner exists; every cycle creates a fresh input and leaves it in the widget DisposableStore.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: createInput runs per edit, DisposableStore uses a strong Set, and teardown does not delete the registered values.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The retained size per disposed editor depends on implementation details, while the one-or-more retained object graphs per edit is certain.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable cleanup-lifecycle regression: disposed inline editors and associated scopes remain strongly retained.

Scenarios.Scenario: Submit an edited historical request, including an active chat editing session
Scenarios.CriticalPath: When an editing session exists, SubmitAction awaits optional configuration persistence and then awaits snapshot restoration before widget.acceptInput can remove later requests and initiate the replacement agent request. Snapshot restore is therefore on the submit critical path; agent execution begins afterward.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Persist the 'do not ask again' confirmation setting when selected
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one write per confirmed edit submission, only when the checkbox is selected.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Normal chat submission did not write this edit-removal preference.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Awaited before snapshot restore and request submission.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Restore/reset modified working-set entries from the selected request snapshot, including restore-to-disk operations
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Up to one reset for each current entry absent from the snapshot and one serial restore for each snapshot entry.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Ordinary SubmitAction did not restore an editing-session snapshot before accepting input; dedicated undo actions could invoke the pre-existing restore API separately.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The new SubmitAction call awaits all entry restoration before acceptInput and the replacement request can proceed.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Invoke the selected chat agent for the replacement request
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One logical agent invocation per submitted replacement request.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Every normal submitted chat request already performed one agent invocation.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Starts after snapshot restoration; response progress depends on it, while sendRequest returns its created-response state asynchronously.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of working-set entries in/currently outside the selected snapshot, followed by one replacement request.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Snapshot entries are reset/restored serially with await per entry. The replacement send creates one logical asynchronous agent invocation; blocked request removal is synchronous and downstream model events are accumulated.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Snapshot lookup uses in-memory linear history, but restoring entries still performs per-entry work; there is no cold/warm cache distinction that removes the restore. Agent selection/history behavior is unchanged.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for placement and cardinality; user-visible duration depends on modified-file count and storage speed.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Working-set size and disk latency vary. The serial boundary is intentional to preserve edit semantics, so it was not reported independently.
Scenarios.Verdict: No separate finding: the new restore boundary is required by edit semantics and is serialized intentionally; the reported regressions are avoidable work/retention around this workflow.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 17 changed files and all diff pages. Submitted three findings: unchanged-response reparsing on checkpoints, virtualized request-hover retention, and widget-lifetime retention of per-edit inline inputs.

Stats.CostNote: Copilot SDK reports nano-AI units and model billing multipliers; it does not provide a USD conversion.
